q: In the rubber-hand illusion, what helps a visible fake hand start to feel like part of your own body?
a: Matching brushstrokes on the real and fake hands
d: Synchronized touch on a hidden real hand and a visible rubber one can produce a feeling of ownership over the rubber hand.
s: Flögel and colleagues · Rubber-hand and rubber-foot experiment
choices: Matching brushstrokes on the real and fake hands
Simply painting both hands the same color
Warming the fake hand while cooling the real one
evidence: Abstract reports synchronous stimulation induced ownership; a temporal mismatch of ±0.5 seconds did not.

q: Vibrating an arm tendon while a person holds their own nose can create which bizarre sensation?
d: Conflicting signals about arm position and touch can make the nose seem to stretch. Researchers call this the Pinocchio illusion.
s: Pinocchio Illusion Questionnaire · Primary research
evidence: Introduction describes biceps tendon vibration with the finger touching the nose producing illusory nose elongation.

q: In Aristotle’s touch illusion, one small object touching crossed fingertips can seem like what?
d: Crossing the fingers can confuse the usual mapping of touch. One object can be felt as two despite unchanged physical contact.
s: Cerebral Cortex · Tactile-object mapping experiment
evidence: Abstract explicitly defines Aristotle illusion as one object between crossed fingers perceived as two lateral objects.

q: A thermal grill combines harmless warm and cool bars under the hand. What surprising sensation can the combination produce?
d: The warm and cool signals together can feel painfully hot even though the individual bars are not dangerously hot.
s: Stanford University · Haptic perception lecture
choices: Rapid alternation between hot and cold
evidence: Stanford lecture describes interlaced warm and cool bars eliciting burning heat; cites Craig et al., Science 1994.

q: Two objects weigh exactly the same, but one is much smaller. In the classic size–weight illusion, which generally feels heavier?
d: Perceived heaviness is influenced by size expectations, so equal mass does not guarantee equal felt weight.
s: Saccone and colleagues · Size, weight, and expectations
choices: Whichever is held in the dominant hand
evidence: Primary paper abstract states that the larger of equally weighted objects feels lighter.

q: In the “cutaneous rabbit” illusion, taps at separated points on the skin can seem to do what?
a: Hop through the untouched space between them
d: Rapidly timed taps can be felt at intermediate places that were never actually tapped. The rabbit is an illusion of touch.
s: Geldard and Sherrick · The cutaneous rabbit
choices: Hop through the untouched space between them
Continue for minutes after tapping stops
Turn into a continuous hot sensation
evidence: 1972 Science abstract describes phantom tactile impressions filling the space between stimulated skin locations.

q: After pushing an arm outward against an immovable support, what odd movement can occur when the person relaxes?
d: The Kohnstamm phenomenon is an involuntary aftercontraction following sustained effort. Its mechanisms remain a subject of research.
s: De Havas and colleagues · Kohnstamm phenomenon review
choices: The fingers curl into a fist
evidence: Review introduction describes involuntary arm elevation after an isometric contraction, including pushing against a doorframe.

q: You glance quickly at a clock and its second hand seems frozen for an unusually long moment. What has apparently stretched?
a: The first moment after your eyes land
d: This stopped-clock illusion is called chronostasis. The first viewed interval after a quick eye movement can seem longer than it really is.
s: Yarrow and colleagues · Saccadic chronostasis
choices: The first moment after your eyes land
The moment just before each blink
Only the time spent looking away
evidence: Abstract identifies chronostasis as subjective temporal lengthening of the first visual stimulus after a saccade.

q: Researchers made completely dry surfaces feel damp in a moisture-free chamber. Which property did they vary?
d: Cold touch can contribute to a sensation of wetness even without water. Human wetness perception combines cues rather than relying on a known dedicated wetness receptor.
s: Psychophysical study of moisture-free wetness perception
evidence: Thirty-adult primary experiment varied thermal stimulation in a moisture-free chamber and measured perceived dampness/wetness; reviewed mechanism also supported by PMID28123008.

q: Cambridge’s wearable robotic “Third Thumb” is strapped beside the hand. Which body parts control it through pressure sensors?
d: Pressure under the feet controls the extra thumb, leaving the natural fingers available to work alongside it.
s: University of Cambridge · Third Thumb
evidence: University report describes sensors under the big toes; right and left foot pressure control different thumb movements.

q: Durham researchers trained both blind and sighted adults to judge objects without vision by listening to echoes of what?
d: Participants practiced human echolocation over ten weeks. Reflected sound helped them judge shapes and navigate without relying on sight.
s: Durham University · Learning echolocation
evidence: University report describes twelve blind and fourteen sighted participants learning shape and navigation tasks using clicking sounds without vision.

q: A 20-person listening study found that a difficult podcast task activated vestigial muscles normally associated with moving what?
d: Electrical recordings detected extra activity in muscles above the ears during the hardest listening condition. This does not mean people visibly swivel their ears like cats.
s: Schroeer and colleagues · Effortful listening and auricular muscles
evidence: Abstract: twenty participants; superior auricular muscle activity rose in hardest competing-speaker condition. Posterior auricular activity tracked direction instead.

q: In a lightproof room, a 2009 experiment’s ultrasensitive camera recorded a faint spontaneous glow from which unlit subjects?
d: The light was far too weak for naked eyes. The researchers linked this ultraweak emission to biochemical processes, rather than ordinary infrared heat imaging.
s: Kobayashi and colleagues · Ultraweak photon emission
evidence: Primary abstract and methods report cooled CCD images of five male volunteers; photon emission about1000 times below naked-eye sensitivity. Thermography measured separately.

q: In grip experiments, water-wrinkled fingertips let people use less force to hold which objects securely than smooth wet fingertips did?
d: A study comparing dry, wet and wrinkled fingers found more efficient grip with wrinkled fingertips under wet conditions. That supports, rather than proves, a possible grip-related advantage.
s: Davis · Water-induced finger wrinkles and grip efficiency
evidence: Primary abstract compares grip conditions; wrinkled-finger grip efficiency exceeded wet-unwrinkled and resembled dry control.

q: A sensitive microphone in an ear canal can detect faint sounds generated by what unexpected source?
d: These are otoacoustic emissions: the ear can produce tiny sounds as well as receive them.
s: National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders · Otoacoustic emissions
evidence: NIH glossary defines otoacoustic emissions as low-intensity sounds produced by the inner ear and measurable by a sensitive ear-canal microphone.

q: To test human scent-tracking, Berkeley researchers had blindfolded volunteers crawl along a grassy trail smelling of what?
d: Many volunteers could follow the scented trail, and practice improved tracking. Two open nostrils worked better than one blocked nostril.
s: University of California, Berkeley · Two nostrils better than one
evidence: First-party report describes10-meter string soaked in chocolate essence; improved trained performance and two-nostril advantage.

q: In a GPS-tracked study, people trying to walk straight without a reliable directional cue often followed what unexpected paths?
d: Blindfolded walkers also circled, without a consistent left-or-right bias. The results favored accumulating directional uncertainty over one leg being stronger.
s: Max Planck Society · Walking in circles
evidence: Institutional report: sun or moon visible supported straight course; cloud cover/blindfolding produced circles. Direction not systematic, undermining leg-asymmetry account.

q: In robot-mediated self-tickling experiments, what alteration made a person’s own touch feel more ticklish?
a: A short delay before the robot delivered the touch
d: The delay disrupts the match between a movement and its predicted sensory result. Predictable self-produced touch is usually felt less strongly.
s: Sarah-Jayne Blakemore · Explanation of her self-tickling research
choices: A short delay before the robot delivered the touch
Perfectly matching both movements in time
Slowing both hands together without a delay
Making the robot’s path more predictable
evidence: Researcher-authored explanation says robotic studies inserted small delay between movement and tickle; delay increased ticklishness. UCL thesis independently gives300ms condition.

q: In a visual-imagination experiment, vividly picturing a bright shape could cause which real bodily response even without extra light?
d: Imagined brightness changed pupil size in participants with visual imagery. Participants with aphantasia lacked this imagery-linked light response, although their pupils still responded to actual light.
s: UNSW Sydney · Pupils and visual imagination
evidence: University account describes42imagery participants; imagined bright/dark shapes produced appropriate constriction/dilation; aphantasic group lacked brightness-dependent imagery response.

q: In a 2021 study, some people answered simple questions while still lucid dreaming. How did they send replies to the researchers?
d: Researchers confirmed REM sleep and sometimes received correct real-time answers. Most attempted exchanges did not produce a clear correct response.
s: Northwestern University · Opening a dream dialogue
evidence: Institutional account specifies eye movements/facial twitches; original study table158trials29correct96noresponse. Scope intentionallysome,notuniversal.

q: When a familiar sign was “on the tip of the fingers,” which part of its form was least readily recalled in a study of deaf signers?
d: A forgotten sign could leave fragments behind: handshape, location or orientation were more accessible than movement. Partial retrieval is not limited to spoken words.
s: Thompson, Emmorey and Gollan · Tip-of-the-fingers study
evidence: 2005primary abstract: TOF signers sure they know sign but cannot retrieve it, often partial phonology, spontaneous resolution.

q: In people blind from birth, research has found that spoken language can recruit brain regions usually associated with which other ability?
d: Parts of the occipital cortex can participate in language processing without visual experience. Brain functions are not assigned as rigidly as a simple diagram suggests.
s: Bedny and colleagues · Language processing in the occipital cortex
evidence: Primary paper: congenitally blind left visual cortex responds to language structure and shows increased connectivity with language regions. Avoids claiming all cortex rewired.

q: In the nasal cycle, what changes inside the nose to let airflow dominance shift between the nostrils?
d: This is the nasal cycle. Swelling and shrinking tissue changes airflow, though real patterns are often less regular than a perfectly alternating cycle.
s: Kahana-Zweig and colleagues · Measuring the human nasal cycle
choices: The septum swinging from side to side
The nostrils sealing on alternate breaths
evidence: Primary33-person24h airflow study describes alternating nostril obstruction by erectile tissue. Irregularity qualified with later primary PMID34432862.

q: A face photograph has its eyes and mouth flipped within the face. Which change can make the grotesque alteration much harder to notice?
a: Turning the whole photograph upside down
d: The Thatcher illusion shows how orientation changes our perception of facial features. The odd expression becomes striking when the whole face is upright.
s: Psalta and colleagues · Thatcher illusion study
choices: Turning the whole photograph upside down
Converting the photograph to black and white
evidence: Primary abstract: participants discriminated normal/Thatcherized upright faces but not inverted; eye/mouth regions orientation-sensitive. York author PDF explicitly describes feature reversal.

q: In the McCollough illusion, black-and-white striped patterns can acquire apparent colors linked to which feature?
d: Color aftereffects can become tied to stripe orientation. Unlike a fleeting ordinary afterimage, the McCollough effect can persist for days or longer under experimental conditions.
s: Allan and Siegel · McCollough-effect experiments
choices: The direction of the room’s lighting
evidence: Primary abstract describes orientation-contingent color on grids, orthogonal orientation relation. Long persistence independently read in Jones/Holding1975 PMID1185119, including up to2040hours.

q: In a famous attention experiment, people counting basketball passes often missed someone walking through the scene dressed as what?
d: Concentrating on the passes could make an unexpected visitor go unnoticed. The demonstration illustrates inattentional blindness, rather than poor eyesight.
s: Simons · Research on the gorilla attention demonstration
evidence: Author’s follow-up paper discusses original gorilla experiment, chest-thumping visitor and selective attention; original Simons/Chabris1999 paper also read.

q: During a real-world conversation experiment, some pedestrians failed to notice which remarkable switch?
a: The person talking to them was replaced
d: A brief visual interruption allowed a different experimenter to take over. The study showed that change blindness can occur during a live interaction.
s: Simons and Levin · Real-world change blindness
choices: The person talking to them was replaced
The speaker repeated every sentence backward
evidence: 1998primary abstract: experimenter initiated conversation, surreptitiously replaced, only half pedestrians noticed.

q: If a cough replaces a speech sound in a recorded sentence, listeners may believe they heard what?
d: This is phonemic restoration. In the original experiment, a silent gap was easier to locate than a gap filled with an interrupting sound.
s: Warren · Perceptual restoration of missing speech sounds
choices: A higher-pitched version of every word
evidence: Primary abstract directly contrasts cough/tone replacement causing illusory missing phoneme with correctly detected silence.

q: An odd recording of “sine-wave speech” may initially sound like whistles. What can suddenly make the same recording intelligible?
a: Hearing the original clear sentence first
d: Prior knowledge can make words pop out of the unchanged degraded sound. The listener’s interpretation changes even though the recording does not.
s: Matt Davis, MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit · Sine-wave speech
choices: Hearing the original clear sentence first
Playing it slightly faster each time
Removing every pause between the sounds
evidence: Researcher’s institutional demonstration explicitly contrasts naive whistles/science-fiction perception with clear-sentence priming and intelligible replay.

q: Across many languages, people tend to pair the made-up word “kiki” with what sort of shape?
d: The bouba–kiki effect links sound and shape: kiki usually feels sharp, while bouba feels rounded. The association is widespread, but not universal.
s: University of Birmingham · Cross-language bouba–kiki research
evidence: Researchers’ account of25languages: majority roundedbouba/spikykiki across writing systems; exceptions explicitly acknowledged.

q: In a “choice blindness” experiment, people sometimes explained why they preferred a face photograph that had actually been what?
a: Secretly swapped for the one they rejected
d: Some participants missed the switch and gave reasons for a choice they had not made. The result shows a gap between choosing and explaining a choice.
s: Johansson and colleagues · Choice blindness experiment
choices: Secretly swapped for the one they rejected
Turned upside down in full view
Removed before they ever saw it
evidence: Primary Science2005 report: attractiveness choices betweenfacepairs; concealed mismatch between intendedchoice andpresentedoutcome; reasons offered despitefailuretonotice.

q: In a Reading study, which simple activity reduced reports of a catchy song repeating in participants’ minds?
d: Gum-chewers reported fewer musical intrusions than control conditions. The proposed link involves the movement planning used for inner speech; it is not a guaranteed earworm cure.
s: University of Reading · Gum-chewing and earworms
evidence: Institutional study report98volunteers, gum fewerthoughts/heardmusic than noactivity andfingertapping controls; primaryabstract DOI10.1080/17470218.2015.1034142 also read.

q: In a 2003 case study, particular combinations of speech sounds consistently triggered which unusual sensation?
d: Lexical–gustatory synesthesia links language with taste. A studied individual had consistent taste associations with particular combinations of speech sounds.
s: Ward and Simner · Lexical–gustatory synesthesia
choices: A shift in the apparent position of the body
evidence: Single-case primary study: speech sounds produced involuntary tastes subjectively locatedinmouth; structured phoneme/taste relationships. Avoids claiming allwords/allpeople.

q: Which task is typically slowed by the Stroop effect?
a: Naming ink colors when the printed words name different colors
d: The Stroop effect exposes a conflict between reading and color naming. A familiar word can interfere even when its meaning is irrelevant to the task.
s: Wheeler · Interference in the Stroop test
choices: Naming ink colors when the printed words name different colors
Reading color words printed in black
Naming colors shown as solid patches
Reading words whose ink colors match their meanings
evidence: 36-college-student primary experiment verbalinknaming slower thanwordreading, supports verbalresponseinterference. Genericdefinition also confirmed PMID9268815.

q: After studying words such as bed, rest and awake, people in a classic memory experiment often “remembered” which word that had never appeared?
d: Related words can activate a missing theme word strongly enough to create a confident false memory. The effect was demonstrated with carefully constructed word lists.
s: Roediger and McDermott · Creating false memories
evidence: Primary1995abstract explicitly usesbed/rest/awake associates ofomittedsleep, false recall andhighconfidencerecognition.

q: For people with the photic sneeze response, which unexpected event can trigger a sneeze?
a: A sudden increase in bright light
d: Some people sneeze when moving into bright sunlight. The mechanism is still debated; it is not simply dust entering the nose.
s: Langer and colleagues · Neural study of photic sneezing
choices: A sudden increase in bright light
Seeing the color blue in dim light
evidence: PrimaryEEGstudy introduction establishes brightlight-associated sneeze/prickling; comparative corticalresults, noexactmechanismclaimed. Laterreview PMID39893297 confirmsuncertainty.

q: In some people, stimulating the outer ear canal can unexpectedly trigger which reflex?
d: The ear-cough reflex involves the auricular branch of the vagus nerve. An ear stimulus can therefore set off a response usually associated with the airway.
s: Dicpinigaitis and colleagues · Arnold nerve reflex study
evidence: Primary study defines Arnoldreflex as cough from externalearcanal stimulation, auricularvagus. No self-testing instructions orprevalencegeneralizations.

q: Identical twins can share virtually the same inherited DNA yet still differ in which familiar identification feature?
d: Fine details of fingerprint ridges are shaped by development in the womb as well as genes. Identical twins do not have identical prints.
s: MedlinePlus Genetics · How fingerprints form
evidence: NIHgenetics page explicitlydifferent identical-twinfingerprints,environmental/intrauterinedevelopmentandgenes.

q: NC State researchers found thousands of microbial genetic types across samples from which small, often-overlooked body feature?
d: The navel survey found great microbial variety across participants. Only a small set of types was widespread, while many occurred in very few samples.
s: NC State University · Belly Button Biodiversity findings
evidence: Institutionalreport2368phylotypes acrossnavelsamples; manyfoundonceortwice andfewwidespread. Doesnotcallallnew species orimplythousandspernavel.

q: What can persist in a mother’s tissues for years after childbirth as a result of fetal microchimerism?
a: A small population of her child’s cells
d: Cells can cross between mother and fetus during pregnancy. Persisting fetal cells are one example of microchimerism: genetically different cells coexisting in one body.
s: National Cancer Institute · Chimerism
choices: A small population of her child’s cells
A reserve of unused pregnancy hormones
A stored supply of fetal blood plasma
evidence: NCIdefinition says fetal cellsabsorbedintoblood andDNAcanpersistintissuesmanyyearsafterchildbirth; nohealthbenefitclaims.

q: When researchers filmed knuckles cracking inside an MRI scanner, what appeared rapidly in the joint fluid?
d: The cavity formed as joint surfaces separated. The imaging linked the crack to this event, rather than bones snapping against each other.
s: University of Alberta · MRI knuckle-cracking study
evidence: 2015firstparty MRIreportrapidgasfilledcavitycreation synovialfluid eachcrack; nohealthorhabitualcrackadvice.

q: A Brown sleep study found a “night watch” effect during the first night in unfamiliar surroundings. What was unusually uneven?
a: Sleep depth between parts of the two brain hemispheres
d: One side showed lighter sleep and stronger responses to unexpected sounds in a measured network. The finding does not mean an entire half-brain remained fully awake.
s: Tamaki and colleagues · First-night sleep effect
choices: Sleep depth between parts of the two brain hemispheres
evidence: PrimaryabstractregionalDMNinterhemisphericsleepdepthasymmetryfirstsession; shallowerhemisphereenhanceddeviantresponse. Carefullynotwholesaleunihemisphericsleep.

q: A gene variant associated with dry earwax also affects production of which surprisingly separate personal trait?
d: ABCC11 influences both earwax type and the secretions behind characteristic underarm odor. The connection is genetic, not caused by moving wax elsewhere.
s: University of Bristol · ABCC11 and odor research
evidence: InstitutionalreportABCC11variant drywax andlow/absent characteristicaxillaryodor; primaryPMC3674910abstractread. Nohygieneadvice.

q: Inherited differences in odor detection help explain why some people cannot smell a distinctive urine odor after eating which vegetable?
d: Research found differences in both odor production and detection. Some people are less able to smell the characteristic compounds, with a genetic association involving smell receptors.
s: Monell researchers · Asparagus odor production and perception
evidence: Forcedchoiceprimaryexaminedproductionandperceptionseparately; individualdifferencesinboth, geneticassociationwithperception. Avoidsclaimallproduceorthereisoneuniversalvariant.

q: Chemical growth records in baby teeth have helped researchers reconstruct which event from infancy?
d: Changing barium levels in tooth layers track early dietary transitions. Researchers checked the method against known feeding histories before applying it to an ancient tooth.
s: Harvard University · Teeth as records of early diet
choices: The first night of uninterrupted sleep
The first successful attempt at walking
evidence: Universityreport barium patterns correspondingtobreastfeeding/weaningvalidatedknownhumans/macaques. Teethlayergrowthsupportsbriefexplanation.

q: After handshakes, hidden-camera research at Weizmann found an increase in what easily overlooked behavior?
d: The researchers also tested transferred odors. The results suggested a possible scent-sampling role for handshakes, without proving that this is why the custom evolved.
s: Weizmann Institute · The scent of a handshake
evidence: Firstpartyreport increasedhand-sniffingafterhandshake; labpublicationabstract271subjects, odor manipulation support. Wordingavoidsuniversalhandororiginclaim.

q: In a sleep-onset study, even participants with amnesia who could not recall playing a game reported images from which game?
d: Three amnesic participants reported game-like imagery as they fell asleep. Such images could occur despite a lack of conscious memory for playing.
s: Stickgold and colleagues · Replaying the game
evidence: Primary2000Scienceabstract explicitly Tetrisimages sleep onsetincludingthreeamnesicswithoutrecall; notnormalREMdreamrelabel.

q: Under special laboratory conditions, people have perceived near-infrared light through what unusual retinal process?
d: Two lower-energy photons can jointly activate a visual pigment. This controlled effect does not give people ordinary thermal vision.
s: Palczewska and colleagues · Human infrared vision
choices: Heating the retina without activating its pigments
Reflecting infrared into the visible spectrum at the cornea
Switching to a separate infrared-sensitive pigment
evidence: PrimaryPNASstudy psychophysicalIRperception plusbiochemical two-photonvisualpigmentisomerization; no DIYexposureinstructions.

q: In a detailed study of two people with six functional fingers per hand, brain scans found what for the extra finger?
d: Each extra digit had its own muscles and nerves and could move independently. The brain accommodated a further controllable digit in these two participants.
s: Mehring and colleagues · Six-fingered hand abilities
choices: Control only through the toe representation
Complete sharing of the little finger’s representation
evidence: Primaryabstract2subjects extraindependentmuscle/nerves/corticalrepresentation enhancedonehandtasks; noassumptionallpolydactylyfunctional.

q: The BrainPort system converts a camera image into patterns of electrical stimulation delivered to which body part?
d: Users learn to interpret a small grid of tactile signals as information about shapes and objects. It is sensory substitution, not a camera implanted in the eye.
s: Primary BrainPort training study · Sensory substitution
evidence: Apparatussectionheadmountedcamera20x20electrodesintraoraldeviceontongue, shapeidentificationtraining.

q: In a laboratory illusion, a gently tapped hand began to feel harder and stiffer after researchers changed what?
d: Pairing the touches with marble-impact sounds altered the hand’s perceived material qualities. Timing and the kind of sound mattered.
s: Senna and colleagues · Marble-hand illusion
choices: The wording of an unrelated memory task
The temperature of the other hand
evidence: Primaryabstract substitutesmarbleimpactfornaturalhandtapsound; perceivedstiffnesshardnessheavinesschanges; asynchronouscontrolnoeffect.

q: When people located landmarks on their own hidden hands, the resulting mental maps tended to depict what distortion?
d: The position estimates produced a systematically distorted hand shape. Knowing what your hand looks like does not guarantee an accurate internal map used for position sense.
s: Longo and Haggard · Implicit body representation
choices: Uniformly enlarged hands with unchanged proportions
Hands rotated so the thumb changed sides
evidence: Primarypaperabstract10landmarks occludedhand, reliable shortenedfingersbroadenedhands. Notclaimconsciousvisualself-imageidentical.

q: In an audio experiment, boosting high frequencies in the sound of hands rubbing together made the skin feel what?
d: Changing the sound can change perceived skin texture even though the skin itself has not been altered. Cutting those frequencies tends to shift the feeling toward moisture.
s: Primary audiotactile-integration experiment
evidence: Resultssectionhighfrequencyboostdrier,cutmoister incontrolsandCIgroups; originalJousmäki/Hari1998and2011studyalsoidentified.

q: In a Keele experiment comparing four utterances during a cold-water task, which increased pain tolerance?
d: The real swear word outperformed the made-up substitutes in this experiment. Being funny or emotionally noticeable was not enough for the substitutes to reproduce the result.
s: Stephens and Robertson · Conventional versus invented swearing
choices: A neutral word chosen by the participant
evidence: Primary2020study92participants; conventionalfuckincreasedthreshold/toleranceagainstneutral,twizpipe/fouchdidnot. Describesstudy,notmedicaladvice.

q: The DishBrain experiment connected living neurons in a dish to a simplified version of which video game?
d: Electrical signals linked human- or rodent-derived neural cultures to a virtual paddle and ball. The work studied adaptive activity; it did not establish human-like consciousness.
s: Kagan and colleagues · DishBrain
evidence: Primary2022Neuron summaryhuman/rodentneurons multielectrodearrayclosedloopPongsimulation. Learningandconsciousnessnotconflated.

q: In an experiment with an itchy right forearm, scratching the left forearm reduced the itch most when participants saw what?
a: A mirror view making the left arm look like the right
d: The visual illusion let scratching on the other arm partly relieve the reported itch. The finding came from controlled experiments, not a general treatment recommendation.
s: Primary study · Itch relief by mirror scratching
choices: A mirror view making the left arm look like the right
An unaltered view of both arms
A close-up of the actual itchy patch
A mirror showing only their face
evidence: Primary2experiments contralateralnonscratcheditchattenuationselectivelymirrorcondition. Scopepartialsubjectiverelief.

q: Repeatedly copying a familiar word can sometimes make it feel strangely unfamiliar. What is this opposite-of-déjà-vu experience called?
d: Researchers induced this feeling through word repetition. Knowing that a word is familiar can coexist with an eerie sense that it suddenly looks wrong.
s: Moulin and colleagues · Laboratory induction of jamais vu
evidence: Primarywordcopyingexperimentsstrangeunfamiliaritydespiteknowledgefamiliarword; calledjamaisvu. Avoidsfixedrepetitioncountinstruction.

q: In a UCLA memory study, only one of 85 participants drew which familiar technology logo completely correctly?
d: Frequent exposure did not guarantee detailed recall. Even recognizing the correct version among alternatives proved surprisingly difficult for many participants.
s: Blake, Nazarian and Castel · Memory for the Apple logo
evidence: Primaryabstract1of85accuraterecallApplelogo, fewerthanhalfrecognition; Apple/PCusergeneralresultsdidnotdiffer.

q: A study of shared false visual memories examined people “remembering” which accessory on the usual Monopoly mascot?
d: The familiar mascot is commonly misremembered with a monocle. Researchers found consistent errors even when people drew some icons from memory.
s: University of Chicago · Visual Mandela effect
evidence: PrimaryinstitutionreportandPMID36219739discussfalsemonocle. Wordingusualmascot avoidsabsoluteeverylicensedvariantneverclaim.

q: In photo-preference research, people tended to prefer which version of their own face, unlike their friends’ usual preference?
d: The result fits familiarity: people often see themselves in mirrors, while friends usually see the unreversed face. It is a group tendency, not everyone’s preference.
s: Mita, Dermer and Knight · Reversed facial images
choices: A version with both halves made identical
evidence: Original1977two-studyabstractmirrorpersonversusnormalfriend;2024primaryPMID39351699replicationalso read.

q: People wearing a potentially embarrassing T-shirt in the “spotlight effect” experiments tended to overestimate what?
a: How many observers would remember the shirt
d: Our own appearance can feel more noticeable to us than it is to other people. The experiments compared wearers’ predictions with observers’ actual recall.
s: Gilovich and colleagues · Spotlight effect
choices: How many observers would remember the shirt
How negatively observers rated the shirt’s wearer
How long observers stared directly at the shirt
How many observers recognized the pictured celebrity personally
evidence: PrimaryabstractStudies1/2T-shirt wearersoverestimatedobserverrecallpicture. No generalmentalhealthadvice.

q: What unusual covering did University of Tokyo researchers attach to a robotic face that could smile?
a: Living skin grown from human cells
d: Anchors inspired by skin ligaments held the cultured tissue to the robot. The demonstration let the skin deform with a smile and return afterward.
s: University of Tokyo · Robots face the future
choices: Living skin grown from human cells
A shell made from human hair
A film of dried collagen without living cells
evidence: Firstparty2024releaseculturedhumanskin perforationanchorsroboticsmilingface; nocompletehumanoidcapabilityclaimed.

q: In an experiment probing the limit of human vision, researchers generated pairs of photons. What happened to the partner of the photon sent toward the eye?
d: Detecting the partner verified that a photon had been produced. Across many trials, the authors reported that participants identified the interval containing the eye-directed photon slightly better than chance.
s: Rockefeller University · Single-photon detection study
choices: It went to the other eye
It was stored in the crystal
It was reflected back at the light source
evidence: Institutionreportandprimarypaperquantumsourceonephotonincidentcornea,abovechance>30ktrials. Plainhumanperceptionscope. Rockefeller full page reopened; line31 confirms partner sent to detector; line33 reports above-chance forced choices.

q: To create the intensely saturated color perception called “olo,” Berkeley’s Oz system selectively stimulated what?
a: One type of retinal cone cell
d: The 2025 experiment targeted M cones in five participants. Ordinary light generally stimulates overlapping cone types, so the unusual pattern produced an unusual color experience.
s: UC Berkeley Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute · Olo
choices: One type of retinal cone cell
The eye’s entire light-sensitive surface uniformly
evidence: Firstpartyfullpage27–30fiveparticipantsretinamappedMconesselectiveactivation; noexactcolorreproductionclaimorDIYinstructions.

q: A study of people newly able to see after congenital blindness tested whether they could immediately identify by sight objects known by what other sense?
d: They could distinguish objects within each sense, but initially struggled to match touch with sight. The cross-sensory link developed quickly after visual experience.
s: Held and colleagues · The newly sighted fail to match seen with felt
evidence: Primary2011abstracthaptictovisualsamplematching lackimmediatetransferrapiddevelopment; fullpaperwithin-sensecontrolsread.

q: The tiny moving lights known as “blue-sky sprites” arise from which cells moving through vessels in the eye?
d: These are part of the blue-field entoptic phenomenon. Their light transmission differs from that of surrounding red blood cells; they are distinct from ordinary floaters.
s: American Academy of Ophthalmology · Blue-field entoptic phenomenon
evidence: OfficialAAOpagefullindexedbodyreadafterdirect403; sourceidentifieswhitecells allowingbluelightthroughvsredabsorption. PrimaryPMID2703307and11980869also read.

q: When the body metabolizes stored fat, most of that fat’s mass eventually leaves by which route?
d: Fat breakdown produces carbon dioxide and water. Most of the original fat mass exits through the lungs; it does not simply turn into heat or muscle.
s: UNSW Sydney · Where metabolized fat goes
evidence: InstitutionauthorsandBMJ2014massbalance:8.4of10kgfatCO2,1.6water. No recommendationtobreathefasterordietadvice.

q: In developmental experiments, some young children thought they could hide themselves merely by concealing what?
d: The children could recognize that their bodies remained visible yet treat their selves as hidden. The researchers linked the pattern to eye contact and developing ideas of self.
s: Russell and colleagues · Young children and self-visibility
evidence: Fourexperiments2–4yearsaffirmselfnotbodyinvisiblewheneyesclosed/hidden; finaleyecontactfinding. Avoidssimpleblindnessmisunderstandingoversimplification.

q: After practice stepping onto a moving platform, participants were explicitly told it had stopped. What happened on their first step onto it?
a: Their bodies still overcompensated for movement
d: A learned movement adjustment can briefly survive conscious knowledge that conditions have changed. Laboratory participants showed the aftereffect even after an explicit warning.
s: Reynolds and Bronstein · Broken-escalator aftereffect
choices: Their bodies still overcompensated for movement
Their movement immediately matched their original stationary-platform steps
They consistently undershot the platform with their leading foot
Their walking speed dropped below their original stationary-platform speed
evidence: 14subjectprimarysledmovingthenstationaryunequivocalwarning; fastwalktrunkovershoot persistedfirsttrial. No broadbalanceadvice.

q: In the autokinetic illusion, a single dim light in an otherwise dark room seems to do what while actually staying still?
d: Without surrounding visual references, a fixed light can appear to move. Researchers have studied the illusion with both perceptual tests and brain imaging.
s: Riedel and colleagues · Imaging autokinesis
choices: Switch repeatedly between red and green
Cast a visible shadow toward the observer
evidence: Primary11subjectfMRIstationarydimLED apparentmotionincreasingwithfixationtime. Mechanismnotclaimedsettled.

q: A mouse study investigating why tattoos persist found that replacement immune cells did what with pigment released by older cells?
d: The pigment could pass through cycles of release and recapture while the tattoo remained. The proposed explanation depends on renewing cells, not one immortal batch of pigment-filled cells.
s: Institut Curie · Tattoo persistence research
choices: Broke all of it into colorless molecules
Transported all of it into the bloodstream
Expelled all of it through the skin surface
evidence: Primary2018JEMabstractmousemodelmacrophagedeletioncapture-release-recapturetattoopersists; clearlyanimalexperimentrelevanthumanprocess.

q: Using synchrotron analysis, researchers found that some particles from human tattoos had traveled beyond the skin to where?
d: The analysis identified tattoo-related pigments in regional lymph nodes. The finding concerns movement and deposition of particles, not proof of a particular health outcome.
s: European Synchrotron Radiation Facility · Tattoo particle transport
evidence: FirstpartyESRFandBfRresearchhumanpigments/TiO2inregionalnodes; healthoutcomesnotinferred.

q: Some skin pigmentation patterns follow the curved lines of Blaschko. These patterns can reveal what hidden biological patchwork?
a: Genetically different populations of skin cells
d: Skin mosaicism can produce streaks and swirls rather than random spots. The pattern reflects the distribution of cell populations established during development.
s: Dermatology research review · Cutaneous mosaicism
choices: Genetically different populations of skin cells
The exact paths of individual veins
The outlines of each underlying muscle
The drainage paths of sweat pores
evidence: Reviewhistoryandembryogenesissectionscelllineageproliferation/mosaicism, geneticconfirmation1994. DoesnotclaimallhumanstripesvisibleunderUV.

q: Rapidly cycling through aligned photographs of ordinary faces can make them appear like what, despite leaving the photos unedited?
d: The flashed-face distortion effect exaggerates features relative to other faces in the sequence. Presentation conditions change perception without digitally warping the portraits.
s: Tangen and colleagues · Flashed-face distortion effect
evidence: Primary2011abstractfastpacedeyealignedfacesseemcaricature/deformed; deviationsrelativeothersaccentuated.

q: Tiny experimental Anthrobots were made from adult human cells normally found in which lining?
d: The cells assembled into moving structures propelled by cilia. In laboratory dishes, clusters also encouraged growth across scratches in a layer of neurons.
s: Tufts University · Anthrobots
evidence: Firstpartyreporttrachealadultcells,noDNAediting,selfassemblyciliaandneurondishscratchgrowth. Laboratoryscopeexplicit. Final peer precision: primary paper bronchial epithelial cells and press tracheal descriptions support general airway lining rather than exact windpipe.

q: A prototype fingertip fuel cell developed at UC San Diego generated electricity while its wearer slept by harvesting what?
d: The device used enzymes to obtain energy from lactate in perspiration. Unlike exercise-powered wearables, its fuel cell could work while the wearer rested.
s: UC San Diego · Fingertip energy harvester
evidence: Institutional report and primary Joule PDF read: lactate biofuel cell, resting and sleeping collection; paper https://xugroup.eng.ucsd.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/08/73_Joule.pdf .

q: In the experimental BrainNet system, what did a receiver perceive when a teammate sent a “rotate the block” instruction through the brain interface?
d: A computer translated a sender’s brain signal into magnetic stimulation of the receiver’s visual cortex. The perceived flash carried a simple instruction; this required specialized equipment.
s: BrainNet primary study
evidence: Primary study read: five triads, EEG senders, TMS recipient; phosphene presence carried rotate instruction.

q: In thermal-taste experiments, warming a previously cooled tongue tip can produce which taste even without sugar?
d: Temperature changes alone induced taste sensations in some participants. Warming the front of the tongue could feel sweet; cooling could produce salty or sour sensations.
s: Cruz and Green · Thermal taste
evidence: Primary abstract read: anterior tongue cooling then warming evokes sweetness; cooling sourness/saltiness. Some people, not universal.

q: Syncytin, a protein that helps human placental cells fuse, was adapted during evolution from what source?
d: An inherited viral envelope gene acquired a new job in placental development. This is an ancient genetic inheritance, rather than a fresh viral infection during pregnancy.
s: Mi and colleagues · Syncytin
evidence: Original Nature abstract read: HERV-W envelope-derived gene, placenta expression, cell fusion and blocking-antiserum evidence.

q: The antibiotic compound lugdunin was discovered in bacteria living in which surprisingly ordinary human location?
d: Researchers found that a nasal Staphylococcus species makes a compound that inhibits competing bacteria. The discovery came from studying our own microbial residents.
s: University of Tübingen · Lugdunin discovery
evidence: Institutional announcement and English press-release PDF read; nasal Staphylococcus lugdunensis, animal and laboratory work, no approved-treatment claim.

q: A study of 60 French and German newborns found a difference in their cries that echoed the melody of their surroundings. Which sound feature differed?
d: French newborns more often produced rising melodic contours, while German newborns more often produced falling ones. The researchers linked the pattern to exposure to language before birth.
s: Mampe and colleagues · Newborn cry melody
evidence: Primary 2009 abstract and methods read: 30 French/30 German newborns aged 2–5 days. Interpretation of prenatal language exposure qualified.

q: In research in the Australian Aboriginal community of Pormpuraaw, people often arranged chronological pictures according to what reference?
d: Some participants organized time from east to west, regardless of which way they faced. A timeline need not be anchored to the viewer’s left and right.
s: Boroditsky and Gaby · Spatial representations of time
choices: Distance toward and away from the viewer
Height above and below the viewer
evidence: Primary abstract read: absolute east–west spatial time arrangement in Pormpuraaw, not universal claim about all speakers.

q: A Russian-English color experiment explored a linguistic boundary between which two colors that English usually groups under one basic color name?
d: Russian distinguishes goluboy from siniy. Russian speakers were faster across this boundary in the experiment, and a simultaneous verbal task removed the advantage.
s: Winawer and colleagues · Russian blues
evidence: Primary abstract and PMC body read: light/dark blue lexical contrast, within/across category comparison and verbal versus spatial interference.

q: In a sleep-learning experiment, tones were paired with pleasant or unpleasant odors. What did participants later do when the tones played without any odor?
d: Sleeping participants learned a simple tone-odor association. Their sniff responses to the tones persisted into waking, without conscious awareness of the learning.
s: Arzi and colleagues · Learning during sleep
choices: Say the name of the odor
Recognize the tone as a familiar melody
evidence: Primary abstract read: partial-reinforcement trace conditioning, pleasant/unpleasant odor-specific sniff amplitudes during sleep and ensuing wake; no complex sleep-learning claim.

q: The faint bow-tie pattern called Haidinger’s brushes reveals that human eyes can detect which property of light?
d: Macular pigments interact differently with differently oriented light. Under suitable conditions, this produces a subtle yellowish-blue pattern even without a visible object in that shape.
s: Haidinger Brush Phenomenon · NCBI Bookshelf
evidence: Institutional medical optics explanation read in full indexed body; polarization and macular pigment mechanism, bow-tie appearance.

q: An EPFL robotic experiment created a spooky feeling by introducing a mismatch between a participant’s movement and touch on their back. What did some participants sense?
d: The robot disrupted the normal agreement between movement and touch. Some participants attributed the sensation to another presence instead of their own actions.
s: Blanke and colleagues · Robot-induced presence
choices: A familiar voice calling their name
evidence: Primary abstract read: master–slave robotic sensorimotor conflict induced feeling of a presence in healthy participants; not supernatural claim.

q: Research on developing fingerprints found that their ridges follow a shortened version of the developmental program for what other skin structure?
d: The ridge-forming cells begin part of a hair-follicle program but stop short of making follicles. Interacting chemical signals organize the ridges into patterns.
s: University of Edinburgh · Fingerprint formation
evidence: Original Cell abstract read: truncated hair-follicle developmental program, no mesenchymal condensate; Turing EDAR/WNT/BMP patterning. Distinct from identical-twin fingerprint fact.

q: In a 2023 experiment, men exposed to women’s emotional tears showed less of which behavior during a competitive laboratory game?
d: The tears had no noticeable odor. Compared with saline exposure, the men showed reduced aggression in the task; this was a controlled experiment, not a universal claim about crying.
s: Agron and colleagues · Tear chemosignals
evidence: Primary abstract and study description read: women’s emotional tears, male recipients, aggression PSAP, saline control, odor-undetectable; avoid universal sex generalization.

q: After using a mechanical grabber, participants in a body-perception experiment judged touches at their elbow and fingertip as if their arm had become what?
d: The tool temporarily altered the brain’s working representation of the arm. The arm itself had not grown, but touch localization and later movements changed.
s: Cardinali and colleagues · Tool use and body schema
evidence: Primary 2009 correspondence summary read: elbow–middle-fingertip touch localization farther apart after mechanical grabber; free-hand kinematic changes.

q: In the Pulfrich illusion, darkening the view through one eye can make a pendulum swinging side to side appear to follow what path?
d: Different visual delays in the two eyes create misleading depth information. The pendulum seems to move toward and away from the viewer as well as sideways.
s: Fleischhauer and colleagues · Pulfrich phenomenon
choices: A vertical circle in a flat plane
A sideways zigzag with sharp corners
evidence: Primary abstract read: neutral-density filters, 65 healthy subjects, apparent elliptical movement measured in depth; mechanism also primary Columbia Pulfrich paper read.

q: A 2021 Stanford brain-interface study produced on-screen text while a participant imagined performing which action?
d: Implanted sensors recorded brain activity associated with attempted handwriting. Software decoded the intended letters even though the participant’s limbs were paralyzed.
s: Stanford Medicine · Mental handwriting
evidence: Firstparty research report read: participant with paralysis imagined handwritten characters, implanted BCI and AI decoding; not unrestricted thought-reading.

q: The memory-related protein Arc can assemble into tiny virus-like packages. What cargo did researchers find these packages could carry between laboratory-grown neurons?
d: Arc forms capsid-like shells and can transfer genetic messages between cells. The experiments revealed an unusual transport mechanism, not an infection spreading through the brain.
s: University of Utah · Arc protein
evidence: Firstparty report fullbody read: Arc selfassembles into capsids packages own mRNA, transfer in cultured mouse neurons; does not claim direct human-memory-transfer.

q: A University of Tokyo two-legged robot reported in 2024 moved using electrically stimulated pieces of what?
d: The robot combined an artificial skeleton with living muscle tissue. It could walk and pivot underwater; the muscle would dry out in air.
s: University of Tokyo · Biohybrid walking robot
evidence: Firstparty report read: skeletal muscle units, independently stimulated walking/pivoting, underwater limitation. Distinct from skin-covered face and ciliated Anthrobots.

q: In a small study of two people with severe amnesia, what happened when another meal was offered shortly after one they had forgotten eating?
d: Both patients ate from successive meals despite having eaten recently. The finding helped show that memory of a meal can contribute to the regulation of eating.
s: Rozin and colleagues · Memory and multiple-meal eating
choices: They ate only foods missing from the first meal
They correctly described the first meal as soon as they tasted food
evidence: Author-hosted primary PDF read: two densely amnesic patients, repeated sessions successive meals, controls refused; explicit tiny clinical sample.

q: In a study of 32 Turkish-English bilinguals, taboo words produced a stronger skin-conductance response when presented in which language?
d: The participants reacted more strongly to taboo words and childhood reprimands in Turkish than in later-learned English. Emotional force can differ across a person’s languages.
s: Harris and colleagues · Bilingual taboo words
choices: Whichever language appeared second in the test
Whichever language had the longer word
evidence: Author-hosted 2003 primary PDF abstract read: 32 Turkish L1/English L2, skin electrodes, greater autonomic response taboo/reprimands in L1; qualified sample.

q: In an experiment involving a simulated walk through rooms, when did recognition memory start to worsen around a doorway?
d: Seeing an upcoming doorway reduced recognition memory in the experiment, even before crossing it. The researchers controlled for elapsed time, distance, surprise, and visual complexity.
s: Primary study · Anticipated event boundaries
choices: Only after entering the next room
Only after returning to the original room
Only after passing through a second doorway
evidence: Primary abstract read: recognition of pseudowords after immersive simulated walk; impairment before boundary, controls. No claim all real doorways always cause forgetting.

q: In a 2025 study, fingertips were soaked on separate occasions and their wrinkles compared. What did the researchers find about the wrinkle patterns?
a: They tended to recur in similar places
d: The wrinkle orientations were more consistent than random patterns. The researchers linked this repeatability to the stable arrangement of blood vessels beneath the skin.
s: Laytin and German · Repeated water wrinkles
choices: They tended to recur in similar places
They reversed their orientation each time
They shifted systematically from tip toward palm
They matched the opposite hand more closely than the same finger
evidence: Primary abstract read: photographs overlaid at two timepoints, vector-orientation correlations versus randomized controls; no exact immutable-pattern claim. Different fact from wet grip.

q: Participants in a frightening free-fall experiment remembered their fall as unusually long. What did a flashing-digit test reveal about their vision during the fall?
a: It did not resolve faster flashes
d: The feeling of extra time was not accompanied by better visual time resolution. The researchers suggested that how the event was remembered helped explain the apparent slowdown.
s: Stetson and colleagues · Fright and perceived time
choices: It did not resolve faster flashes
It resolved flashes far faster than before
It lost the ability to distinguish any digits
It reversed the perceived order of the flashes
evidence: Primary abstract and figure read: 31m controlled fall onto net, LED temporal resolution no improvement, retrospective duration longer; no stunt instructions.

q: In research on why a return journey can feel shorter, what happened when cyclists returned by a different but equally long route?
a: The shorter-feeling return trip still occurred
d: The effect did not require retracing a familiar route. The researchers proposed that expectations about the outward trip helped shape later judgments of travel time.
s: Van de Ven and colleagues · Return-trip effect
choices: The shorter-feeling return trip still occurred
The return trip consistently felt twice as long
Only cyclists who recognized the new route showed the effect
evidence: Primary abstract read: three studies, cycling different equidistant return route preserved effect; expectation interpretation qualified.

q: In a human brain-recording study, what weakened when participants switched from breathing through the nose to breathing through the mouth?
a: The coupling of breathing and brain rhythms
d: The study recorded breathing-linked activity in olfactory and limbic regions. Diverting airflow to the mouth reduced the coupling, showing that the route of breathing mattered.
s: Zelano and colleagues · Breathing and brain rhythms
choices: The coupling of breathing and brain rhythms
The response to changes in breathing depth alone
The timing of brain waves relative to the heartbeat
The neural response to the sound of breathing alone
evidence: Primary abstract read: intracranial EEG in epilepsy patients and separate behavioral study; nasal-versus-oral coupling, no breathing-treatment recommendation.

q: Researchers made an experimental yarn for weaving tissue-engineering materials from sheets of what?
d: Adult human fibroblasts produced the biological sheets. Strips became yarn that could be assembled into strong structures, including experimental vascular grafts.
s: Magnan and colleagues · Human textiles
evidence: Original abstract read: normal human fibroblast cell-assembled extracellular matrix, sheets to yarn, woven vascular grafts. Not weaving intact skin from donors.

q: University of Cape Town researchers grew experimental bricks at room temperature using sand, bacteria, and which human waste product?
d: Bacteria break down urea, helping calcium carbonate cement the sand together. The resulting bio-bricks avoid the kiln-firing stage of ordinary clay bricks.
s: University of Cape Town · Urine bio-bricks
evidence: Official 2018 release read: actual human urine, bacterial urease, calcium carbonate and sand, room-temperature molds.

q: A Harvard biohybrid fish described in 2022 swam using human stem-cell-derived cells of which type?
d: Alternating contractions on its two sides bent the artificial fish back and forth. The device explored principles of muscular pumps; it was not a living fish with human organs.
s: Harvard SEAS · Biohybrid fish
evidence: Institutional report and original PMID35143298 read: human-derived cardiac cells, two-layer antagonistic contractions, autonomous swimming. Distinct from electrically stimulated skeletal-muscle walker.

q: Wind-tunnel experiments with model eyelashes found that excessively long lashes could have what surprising effect?
a: Channel more airflow toward the eye
d: Intermediate-length lashes protected the model eye best. Very long lashes could direct air toward its surface, increasing evaporation instead of continually improving protection.
s: Amador and colleagues · Eyelash aerodynamics
choices: Channel more airflow toward the eye
Keep reducing airflow as their length increased
Leave airflow unchanged while blocking more particles
Redirect airflow only along the eyelid rather than toward the eye
evidence: Original abstract and results read: 22 mammal measurements plus models, length optimum, overlong lashes channel high-energy airflow to ocular surface. Experimental model scope.

q: Patients with severe memory impairment could improve at which task despite poor recollection of the practice sessions?
a: Tracing a pattern seen in a mirror
d: The skill could improve and persist despite poor recall of the practice sessions. This helped demonstrate that learning a skill and remembering an event can come apart.
s: Gabrieli and colleagues · Mirror-tracing skill
choices: Tracing a pattern seen in a mirror
Recounting the order of recent events
evidence: Primary abstract read: AD/global-amnesia groups acquired/retained mirror-tracing comparable to controls despite poor recall/recognition; one AMN retained overyear. No claim all amnesia same.

q: In experiments using a computerized balloon-risk game, which basic taste was associated with more risk-taking?
d: Participants sampled taste solutions before playing a computerized balloon game. Across experiments in the UK and Vietnam, sour taste was associated with a greater willingness to risk the game’s rewards.
s: Vi and Obrist · Taste and risk-taking
evidence: Primary abstract/figure read: five taste groups and water, Balloon Analogue Risk-Taking task, three experiments UK/Vietnam. Laboratory scope explicit.

q: People listening attentively to the same story can show correlated fluctuations in which bodily measure, even without interacting?
d: A narrative study found that listeners’ heart-rate changes could track one another. Distraction reduced this synchrony, and stronger synchrony was associated with better story recall.
s: Pérez and colleagues · Narrative and heart-rate synchrony
evidence: Original abstract read: auditory/audiovisual narrative intersubject heart-rate correlation, distraction and recall; not exact beat-for-beat synchronization or interpersonal telepathy.

q: When people watched the same short video stories, their blinks often synchronized at which moments?
d: Blinks clustered around implicit pauses, such as the end of an action. The pattern was not simply a response to every cut between camera shots.
s: Nakano and colleagues · Synchronized eyeblinks
choices: The loudest sound in each scene
The beginning of every spoken sentence
evidence: Primary fullabstract/results read: within/between subjects synchronization, not explicitly tied scene cuts; low-attention scenes and absence main character; backgroundvideo/audio story controls.

q: Human egg cells activated in laboratory experiments released a burst of which metal, visualized with fluorescent probes?
d: The so-called zinc spark is a coordinated release of ions. Researchers used chemical or molecular activation methods; it was not an ordinary visible flash from an egg.
s: Duncan and colleagues · Human egg activation
evidence: Original abstract read: calcium-ionomycin, ionomycin or hPLCζ cRNA activation, selective fluorescent probes, zinc release; avoid unsupported natural fertilization visible-flash claim.

q: Duke researchers found that shifting your eyes while keeping your head still also produces tiny movements in which structures?
d: The movements occurred even without sound, and could begin just before the eyes moved. The finding suggests coordination between the machinery of vision and hearing.
s: Duke University · Eye and eardrum movements
evidence: Institutional fullreport and primary PMID29363603 read: human and monkey saccade-related eardrum oscillations, even withoutsounds and beginsbeforeeye movement.

q: A fingertip-inspired sensor suggested that fingerprint ridges help fine-texture perception by selecting and amplifying what?
d: As ridges move across a textured surface, they shape the vibration pattern. The prominent frequencies can fall in the range detected efficiently by touch-sensitive nerve endings.
s: Scheibert and colleagues · Fingerprints and touch
evidence: Primary abstract read: biomimetic sensor ridges, scanning speed/interridge spacing spectral selection; functional interpretation qualified, not directly human experiment.

q: During a guided museum-tour study, photographing an entire object was followed by what result compared with simply observing it?
d: Participants later remembered fewer objects and details in that condition. Zooming in for a more focused photograph removed the impairment in a second experiment.
s: Henkel · Photo-taking and memory
choices: Better location memory but poorer shape memory
No recognition of any photographed object
evidence: Original two-study abstract read: whole-object photographs impairment for objects/details/location; zoom condition noimpairment. Study-specific not blanket anti-photography advice.

q: In a Yale experiment, adding logically irrelevant information from which field made poor psychological explanations more satisfying to nonexperts?
d: The extra brain-related details did not fix the explanation’s logic. Nevertheless, nonexpert participants rated explanations more favorably when those details were included.
s: Weisberg and colleagues · Seductive neuroscience
evidence: Original abstract read: good/bad explanations with/without irrelevantneuroscience; naiveadults/students butnotexperts showedeffect, strongestbadexplanations.

q: Bone has a tiny piezoelectric response: mechanical and electrical effects are coupled. Which major bone component is a principal contributor?
d: Experiments separating organic and mineral contributions found a much smaller response after removing the organic matrix. Bone’s protein structure can participate in this electromechanical behavior.
s: Keit and Davletkildeev · Bone piezoelectricity
evidence: Primary 2026 abstract read: human cortical bone PFM, NaOCl organic reduction, collagenprincipalcomponent; no biologicalhealing or treatmentclaim.

q: X-rays overturned an early death-date claim for the Mütter Museum’s “Soap Lady” by revealing which hidden evidence?
d: The fasteners were of types not manufactured in the United States until the 1830s. That contradicted an earlier claim that she died during a 1790s epidemic.
s: Mütter Museum · Soap Lady
choices: A dated coin inside the body
A written label under her skull
A maker’s stamp on a coffin plate
evidence: Museum collection page fullread: 1987Xraysbuttons/pins dated1830s disprove1790s, noidentityclaim. Distinctfromadipocereexplanationnotincluded.

q: A study of people blind from birth found that, when speaking to another blind person, they did what with their hand gestures?
d: The speakers had never seen anyone gesture, and their listeners could not see their hands. Gesturing therefore need not depend on copying a visual example or being watched.
s: Iverson and Goldin-Meadow · Why people gesture
choices: They gestured only while touching the listener’s hands
They gestured only after an explicit request
evidence: Primary Nature correspondenceabstract/figure read:12congenitallyblind speakers+sightedcomparisons;4blind speakers withblindexperimenter stillgestured. Smallstudy notuniversal.

q: In experiments on unfamiliar sayings, which wording change made a statement seem more accurate without changing its basic meaning?
d: People rated rhyming versions as more accurate than equivalent nonrhyming versions. The effect shows how the sound of a statement can influence judgments about its truth.
s: McGlone and Tofighbakhsh · Rhyme as reason
choices: Putting it in the past tense
Changing a statement into a question
evidence: Original1999abstractread unfamiliaraphorismrhymingvssemanticallymatchednonrhyming, equalcomprehensibility butrhymingmoreaccurate. No copiedaphorism.

q: In a tactile illusion, moving two parallel metal wires between the palms can make people feel they are touching what kind of surface?
d: People reporting a strong illusion rated the sensation more like leather or fabric than wire. Touch can misidentify a material even when the hands are directly contacting it.
s: Yokosaka and colleagues · Velvet-hand illusion
evidence: Primary abstractread materialcomparisonsstrongillusionleather/fabric, softer/wetter/warmer; stemomitsvelvetnametogiveaway.

q: Research into an old art-conservation technique identified an enzyme in which bodily fluid as an effective cleaning agent?
d: The researchers identified alpha-amylase as the main contributor to saliva’s cleaning power in their tests. They also investigated substitute enzyme preparations.
s: Romão and colleagues · Saliva as a cleaning agent
evidence: Primary abstractread qualitative/chromatography alphaamylase mainsalivacleaning; fullpaperintro goldleaf,paintedceramics conservation. No DIYartcleaninginstruction.

q: Worcester Polytechnic Institute researchers grew beating human heart cells on the stripped-down framework of which vegetable?
d: Removing the plant’s cells left a cellulose scaffold with branching channels. The work was a laboratory proof of concept, not a complete replacement heart.
s: Worcester Polytechnic Institute · Spinach scaffolds
evidence: Institutional fullpageopenedlines207–226: beatinghumancardiac cells spinachdecellularizedleaves, flowmicrobeads, cellulosevascularnetwork; otherplantsuseddifferentexperiments.

q: In a 2015 study, repeated false statements gained credibility even when participants had what?
d: Participants sometimes relied on the ease of processing a repeated claim rather than knowledge already available to them. Familiarity could influence truth ratings despite knowing better.
s: Fazio and colleagues · Knowledge and illusory truth
choices: A reward specifically for believing the statements
Proof that the statements came from an expert
Instructions to assume every statement was correct
evidence: Originaltwoexperimentabstractread: priornormedknowledge/individualposttestdemonstratedknowledge, truthratingsrepeatfalseclaim effect despiteknowledge; noallpeoplealwaysclaim.

q: A tongue-in-cheek randomized trial found no injury benefit from parachutes versus empty backpacks. What crucial detail explains the result?
a: The aircraft were stationary on the ground
d: Participants stepped from very low heights. The study used that absurd contrast to show why the population and circumstances of a trial matter when interpreting its results.
s: BMJ · Parachute randomized trial
choices: The aircraft were stationary on the ground
Every participant landed in deep water
The empty backpacks contained hidden parachutes
Only professional stunt performers were enrolled
evidence: Primary fullabstractread23randomizedfromstationarygroundaircraftmean0.6m0km/h, noinjurybothgroups; satireaboutgeneralizabilityidentified.

q: Four adults in a 2008 study could hear something while watching silent flashes or visual motion. What gave them an advantage on a visual rhythm task?
a: Sound sensations triggered by the images
d: Their cross-sensory experience let them hear as well as see the silent rhythmic patterns. The task used sequences somewhat like visual Morse code.
s: Saenz and Koch · Visually induced auditory synesthesia
choices: Sound sensations triggered by the images
A stronger afterimage after each flash
evidence: Primary correspondence summaryread: fourhearing-motion synesthetes, silentmotion/flashes sounds and bettervisualrhythm discrimination; noactualexternalsound. Differentfromlexicalgustatorysynesthesia33.

q: In the magician’s Criss-Cross force, a spectator freely chooses where to cut a deck. Which card is ultimately presented as their selection?
d: The cut feels like a meaningful choice, but it does not determine the displayed card. Experiments used the trick to study an illusory sense of control.
s: Pailhès and Kuhn · Criss-Cross force
choices: The card exactly halfway down the original deck
The card immediately below the spectator’s cut
evidence: Originalabstractread2020:cutpositiongenuinelyfree alwaysoriginaltopcard; N60/90/60 forcingagencyexperiments. Distinctfromface-photochoiceblindness31:choicecannotaffectoutcome ratherthanswappedoutcomeafterchoice.
